claims.text: Preferential surface segregation of Al and Cr governs the ability of HEAs to develop and retain a protective oxide layer at high temperature.
Surface enrichment in Al and Cr promotes formation of a dense, adherent oxide layer.
A dense, adherent oxide layer inhibits further oxidation.
The proposed initial material is a compositionally homogeneous HEA containing protective-oxide-forming elements such as Al, Cr, or Si.
The proposed intervention is exposure of the HEA to air or another oxygen-rich atmosphere at controlled temperature and duration.
The proposed test range is 800–1200°C for 1–100 hours under controlled oxygen partial pressure.
High-temperature exposure causes selected alloying elements such as Al and Cr to migrate preferentially to the surface.
Surface-segregated Al and Cr react with oxygen to form a stable protective oxide.
The protective oxide limits oxygen diffusion.
The protective oxide limits metal-ion transport.
HEAs with higher Al and Cr concentrations will form more protective oxide layers than HEAs with lower concentrations or without those elements.
HEAs with higher Al and Cr concentrations will exhibit lower oxidation-induced mass gain.
The proposed baseline is a conventional single-phase alloy or an HEA lacking significant Al or Cr, tested under the same oxidation conditions.
The hypothesis applies only when there is sufficient thermodynamic driving force for surface segregation and protective-oxide formation.
The hypothesis applies only over temperatures at which the protective oxides remain stable.
The dependence of surface segregation on alloy composition and processing conditions is not fully understood.
The controlled comparison varies Al and Cr concentrations while holding the high-temperature oxidative exposure conditions identical.
Failure of higher-Al/Cr HEAs to show lower mass gain or to form a dense, adherent oxide relative to lower-Al/Cr HEAs would falsify the hypothesis.
